title: Treatment for acute anterior cruciate ligament tear: five year outcome of randomised trial
question: In young active adults with a new ACL tear, does rehabilitation plus early reconstruction give better five year results than rehabilitation with the option of reconstruction later?

bottom_line.question: In young active adults with a new ACL tear, does rehabilitation plus early reconstruction give better five year results than rehabilitation with the option of reconstruction later?
bottom_line.answer: Knee scores (KOOS4) improved by 42.9 points with early reconstruction and 44.9 points with rehabilitation plus optional later reconstruction, a between group difference of 2.0 points (95% confidence interval −8.5 to 4.5), so early reconstruction did not give better results at five years.

sections.title: Surgery or Rehab First After an ACL Tear?
sections.markdown:
The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is one of the main ligaments that holds the knee together. Tearing it is a common and serious injury in young, active people. Many are offered **ACL reconstruction**, an operation that replaces the torn ligament with a graft taken from one of the patient's own tendons. Doctors disagree about how much that surgery adds to physical rehabilitation, both for how the knee feels and works and for its long-term health. Many people who tear an ACL develop knee osteoarthritis whichever treatment they get.

The authors had already run a randomised trial, called KANON, that compared two treatment strategies. At two years, patients in the two groups rated their knees the same. This report follows the same patients to five years and adds X-ray checks for osteoarthritis and a count of meniscus operations. It is the first randomised trial to compare early surgery with rehabilitation first over this middle-length period.

sections.title: How the Trial Worked and What It Measured
sections.markdown:
The trial enrolled 121 active adults aged 18 to 35 (average age 26) at two Swedish hospitals. Each had torn the ACL no more than four weeks earlier, in a knee that had never been injured before. Professional athletes were excluded, and so were people who were less than moderately active. So were people with certain other serious knee damage, such as a complete tear of a collateral ligament or full-thickness cartilage damage on MRI.

Everyone followed the same structured rehabilitation programme. Patients were then randomly assigned to one of two strategies:

- **Early reconstruction:** 62 patients had surgery within 10 weeks of the injury, as well as rehab.
- **Rehab first, with optional delayed reconstruction:** 59 patients started with rehab alone. They were offered surgery later only if the knee became unstable in a way the protocol defined in advance: giving way caused by the missing ligament, plus a positive "pivot shift" test (a hands-on exam that detects this looseness).

Four experienced knee surgeons did all the operations, using either a patellar tendon graft (from the tendon below the kneecap) or a hamstring tendon graft. Both groups had tears of the meniscus (the knee's cartilage shock absorbers) trimmed or repaired when needed.

Only one patient dropped out before five years, so 120 of the 121 were analysed. Losing so few patients is one of the trial's main strengths.

The main measure was the **KOOS** (Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score), a questionnaire patients fill in about their own knee. It has five subscales: pain, symptoms, function in daily living, function in sport and recreation, and knee-related quality of life. Each runs from 0 (worst) to 100 (best). The trial's summary score, KOOS4, averages four of the five:

KOOS4 = (sum of four subscale scores) / 4

The main outcome was how much that score improved over five years:

change in KOOS4 = KOOS4 at five years - KOOS4 at the start

With 120 patients, the trial had an 80% chance of detecting a 10-point difference between the groups, the gap the authors had set in advance as the one worth detecting.

Other outcomes included:

- a general health survey (SF-36)
- the Tegner activity scale (a 1 to 10 rating of how physically active someone is)
- whether patients returned to their pre-injury activity level
- knee stability on two hands-on tests (Lachman and pivot shift)
- meniscus surgery
- osteoarthritis on standing X-rays

A radiologist who did not know which treatment each patient had received graded the X-rays for bone spurs (osteophytes) and narrowing of the joint space, two standard signs of osteoarthritis.

The results were analysed in two ways. The **full analysis set** compares patients by the group they were randomly assigned to, whatever treatment they ended up having. The as-treated analysis compares them by what they actually received: early surgery, delayed surgery, or rehab alone. The second view matters here because many patients in the rehab-first group later chose surgery.

sections.title: Key Results at Five Years
sections.markdown:
**Who had surgery.** Of the 59 patients assigned to rehab first, 30 (51%) eventually had a delayed reconstruction, seven of them between two and five years after the injury. Over the five years, 61 patients had early surgery, 30 had delayed surgery and 29 were treated with rehab alone.

**How patients rated their knees.** KOOS4 improved by 42.9 points in the early surgery group and 44.9 points in the rehab-first group. After adjusting for starting scores, the gap between groups was 2.0 points (P=0.54). The 95% confidence interval, the range where the true difference plausibly lies, ran from -8.5 to 4.5, so it stays within 10 points either way. The groups did not differ significantly on any single KOOS subscale, the SF-36, the Tegner activity scale or return to pre-injury activity. The as-treated analysis gave the same picture.

**Knee stability.** This was the one clear difference. At five years, knees assigned to early reconstruction were more stable on both the Lachman and pivot shift tests (both P<0.001). Even so, the patients with looser knees reported no worse pain, function or activity.

**Osteoarthritis.** X-rays were available for 113 knees, and none showed osteoarthritis at the start. By five years, 13 knees (12%) had it in the main joint between the thigh bone and shin bone (the tibiofemoral joint), and 22 (19%) had it behind the kneecap (the patellofemoral joint). The two strategies did not differ significantly.

In the as-treated comparison, reconstructed knees showed tibiofemoral osteoarthritis in 11% and patellofemoral osteoarthritis in 23%. Knees treated with rehab alone showed 12% and 8%. Neither difference was statistically significant (P=0.995 and P=0.084). Graft type did matter. Knees rebuilt with a patellar tendon graft had more osteoarthritis behind the kneecap than knees rebuilt with a hamstring graft (P=0.001). The authors suggest two reasons: the patellar tendon can shorten after surgery, which changes how load passes through the kneecap joint, and bone remodelling where the graft was harvested may encourage bone spurs.

**Meniscus surgery.** Over five years, 61 knees (51%) had meniscus surgery: 29 in the early surgery group and 32 in the rehab-first group (P=0.48). A time-to-event analysis, which tracks when each meniscus was first operated on, also found no difference (P=0.77). In an exploratory analysis that counted repeat operations on the same meniscus, the early surgery group had fewer procedures in total.

**Graft ruptures.** Four patients tore their new graft: 3 of 61 early reconstructions (5%) and 1 of 30 delayed ones (3%). Two of them had revision surgery. These rates match the 4.3% seen in a five-year study of 1,415 reconstructed patients.

sections.title: What the Findings Mean
sections.markdown:
Earlier observational studies suggested that delaying reconstruction leads to more meniscus damage, and that surgery protects the knee from later meniscus tears and osteoarthritis. Those studies suffer from confounding by indication: patients who get surgery early differ from those who don't in ways that can affect their outcomes. Random assignment removes that bias. In this trial, the extra meniscus surgery people feared in the rehab-first group did not show up in the number of knees affected.

Surgery is often recommended so that people can return to sport. However, a meta-analysis of 5,770 reconstructed patients found that after about 41 months, only 63% had returned to their pre-injury activity level and 44% to competitive sport. This trial also found only modest return to previous activity, and it was the same after early surgery, delayed surgery and rehab alone.

The authors call the osteoarthritis finding striking. About one knee in five showed osteoarthritis changes just five years after an injury at around age 30, and surgery did not prevent them. This fits earlier work. The authors' own cohort studies found osteoarthritis in 51% of men and 41% of women 12 to 14 years after injury, with no difference by whether the ligament was reconstructed. A 15-year randomised trial also found no treatment-related difference.

The trial's KOOS scores were similar to five-year data from the Swedish ACL registry (1,465 patients, all reconstructed), which suggests the results carry over to typical patients. Patients and doctors knew the treatment assignments after the two-year point. The five-year osteoarthritis analysis was planned in the original protocol, and the radiologist grading the X-rays did not know who had received which treatment.

sections.title: The Bottom Line
sections.markdown: For young, active adults with a fresh ACL tear, starting with rehab and keeping surgery as an option gave the same five-year results as early reconstruction. That held for self-reported knee function, osteoarthritis on X-ray and meniscus surgery. About half of the rehab-first group never needed an operation, and neither strategy showed signs of causing more harm. Early surgery gave only one advantage: better knee stability on physical exam, which patients did not notice in their own ratings. The authors conclude that clinicians and young active patients should consider rehabilitation as a primary treatment option. The findings do not apply to professional athletes or to people who are less than moderately active.

sources.abstract: Objective To compare, in young active adults with an acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear, the mid-term (five year) patient reported and radiographic outcomes between those treated with rehabilitation plus early ACL reconstruction and those treated with rehabilitation and optional delayed ACL reconstruction. Design Extended follow-up of prospective randomised controlled trial. Setting Orthopaedic departments at two hospitals in Sweden. Participants 121 young, active adults (mean age 26 years) with acute ACL injury to a previously uninjured knee. One patient was lost to five year follow-up. Intervention All patients received similar structured rehabilitation. In addition to rehabilitation, 62 patients were assigned to early ACL reconstruction and 59 were assigned to the option of having a delayed ACL reconstruction if needed. Main outcome measure The main outcome was the change from baseline to five years in the mean value of four of the five subscales of the knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score (KOOS4). Other outcomes included the absolute KOOS4 score, all five KOOS subscale scores, SF-36, Tegner activity scale, meniscal surgery, and radiographic osteoarthritis at five years. Results Thirty (51%) patients assigned to optional delayed ACL reconstruction had delayed ACL reconstruction (seven between two and five years). The mean change in KOOS4 score from baseline to five years was 42.9 points for those assigned to rehabilitation plus early ACL reconstruction and 44.9 for those assigned to rehabilitation plus optional delayed reconstruction (between group difference 2.0 points, 95% confidence interval −8.5 to 4.5; P=0.54 after adjustment for baseline score). At five years, no significant between group differences were seen in KOOS4 (P=0.45), any of the KOOS subscales (P≥0.12), SF-36 (P≥0.34), Tegner activity scale (P=0.74), or incident radiographic osteoarthritis of the index knee (P=0.17). sources.sec-characteristics-of-patients-and-trea: Despite several contacts by mail and telephone, one patient assigned to early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction did not attend the five year clinical visit. Consequently, we included 120/121 participants in this five year follow-up report, 61 of whom were assigned to early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and 59 to initial rehabilitation with the option of having a later reconstruction if needed (table 1). Two patients assigned to early reconstruction did not have reconstruction or had less than 10 rehabilitation visits; we excluded them from the as treated analysis but included them in the full analysis set.

Thirty (51%) patients assigned to initial rehabilitation with the option of having a later reconstruction chose to have (and had) a delayed anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction over the five year period (seven in the period between two and five years; median 867 (range 743-1695) days after injury) (fig 1). Fifteen anterior cruciate ligaments were reconstructed using patella tendon procedures and 15 using hamstrings tendon procedures. Over the five year period, 61 patients had an early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, 30 had a delayed reconstruction, and 29 were treated with rehabilitation alone. Of the 91 primary reconstructions performed, 40 used patella tendon procedures and 51 used hamstrings tendon procedures.
sources.sec-patient-reported-outcomes-5/p1: Patient reported outcomes included the knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score (KOOS), the Medical Outcomes Study 36-item short-form health survey (SF-36), and the Tegner activity scale. Consistent with our previous publication, the main outcome of this report was the change from baseline to five years in the mean value of four of the five KOOS subscales (KOOS4). Other outcomes include the crude KOOS4 score, all five separate KOOS subscales, the scores on the SF-36 physical and mental components (all 0-100 scales, worst to best), and the Tegner activity scale score (1-10, lowest to highest) at five years. In addition, we report return to pre-injury activity level as patients who reported similar or higher Tegner activity scale scores at five years compared with their pre-injury scores.
sources.sec-participants-3/p1: We enrolled active adults, 18 to 35 years of age, with an anterior cruciate ligament tear not more than four weeks old to a previously uninjured knee at the departments of orthopaedics at Skåne University Hospital and Helsingborg Hospital, Sweden (table 1). Major exclusion criteria were professional athletes (10 on the Tegner activity score; 0-10, lowest to highest activity level), less than moderately active people (<5 on the same scale), a total collateral ligament rupture, a full thickness cartilage lesion visualised on magnetic resonance imaging, and extensive meniscal fixation. Details of the recruitment process, full inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the randomisation process have been published. All patients provided fully informed written consent to participate in the study.
sources.sec-knee-radiography-and-grading-of-imag: We report presence of radiographic osteoarthritis separately for the tibiofemoral and patellofemoral compartments. In agreement with previous reports, we considered radiographic osteoarthritis to be present if any of the following criteria were achieved in either of the medial or lateral tibiofemoral compartments or in the patellofemoral compartment: joint space narrowing grade 2 or above (tibiofemoral compartment only); sum of the two marginal osteophyte grades from the same compartment 2 or above; grade 1 joint space narrowing in combination with grade 1 osteophytes in the same compartment (tibiofemoral compartment only). For the tibiofemoral compartment, this cut-off approximates to grade 2 radiographic osteoarthritis based on the Kellgren and Lawrence scale.
